text:
This section examines Experiment O —
Transfer across tasks and

sizes from first principles. Keep two
questions separate: does changing

the order change the measured outcome, and
does the proposed

search method beat a matched alternative
at the same distinct-evaluation

budget? O1, cross-task neural transfer:
XOR-v4 versus parity-v4 over 120

shared orderings; correlation r=-0.004,
effectively zero; top-decile overlap

at chance. O2/O3, same-family cross-size
LLM transfer: derive six-module

position effects and use them to score 222
unbiased eight-module

orderings. Result: Spearman 0.665
[0.582,0.725]. Top decile by transferred

score had mean target accuracy 0.900
[0.873,0.925], versus random-pool mean

0.725. Interpretation: transfer was absent
across different neural tasks but

strong across sizes within the same LLM
instruction family. Visual:

one broken correlation plot for XOR→parity
and one upward-trending plot

for n=6→n=8. Now read evidence panel
O-transfer. The axes, units,

and sample are stated on screen. The
sample represented here

is the sample reported in the source. Raw
observations remain

visible wherever the artifact provides
them. Censored observations stay

marked at the cap rather than becoming
invented hitting times,

and sampled landscapes leave unobserved
permutations blank. The supported

finding is: Result: Spearman 0.665
[0.582,0.725]. The broader claim not

established here is: The conclusion is
scoped to the recorded

evaluator, landscape, and budget. This
evidence changed the program as

follows: Carry this constraint into the
next experiment and compare

methods at equal cost. The distinction is
part of the

result. A large ordering effect does not
automatically imply an

evolutionary-search advantage, and
almost-sure convergence does not promise
practical efficiency.
